questions.stem: John, 45, has an 8 mm clean-based H. pylori-positive duodenal ulcer and is starting 14 days of eradication therapy in general practice. You are safety netting before he goes home. Which symptom should prompt him to call 000 or go straight to the emergency department?
options: Loose stools and a metallic taste in the first week of the antibiotics
Mild burning epigastric pain that is still there after 5 days of treatment
Black, sticky, foul-smelling stools, or feeling faint or light-headed
Bloating and a reduced appetite after large or spicy meals
questions.why: Melaena or feeling faint suggests a bleeding ulcer with possible haemodynamic compromise, which needs emergency assessment. Safety netting should name bleeding (haematemesis, coffee grounds, melaena), collapse and sudden severe abdominal pain (perforation).
notes: Diarrhoea and taste disturbance are expected side effects of amoxicillin and clarithromycin; warn him about them, but they do not need the ED.
Symptoms can take time to settle on a PPI; pain that persists or does not improve calls for GP review, not an emergency call.
Bloating and mildly reduced appetite are common in dyspepsia and were present at baseline; they are not a red flag for a complication.

questions.stem: John, 45, finishes 14 days of esomeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin for an H. pylori-positive, uncomplicated duodenal ulcer, then takes the PPI once daily for another 4 weeks. His pain has gone. How should you confirm eradication?
options: Urea breath test at least 4 weeks after antibiotics, PPI stopped 2 weeks before
H. pylori serology at least 4 weeks after antibiotics, taken while continuing the PPI
Repeat gastroscopy with biopsies 8 weeks after he finishes the antibiotics
Urea breath test 1 week after the antibiotics, while still taking the PPI
questions.why: Confirm eradication with a urea breath test (or faecal antigen test) at least 4 weeks after the antibiotics and at least 2 weeks off the PPI. Antibiotics and PPIs suppress the bacteria and can give a false-negative result.
notes: Serology detects antibodies, which stay positive for months to years after eradication, so it cannot confirm cure.
An uncomplicated duodenal ulcer does not need a repeat scope; repeat gastroscopy is for gastric ulcers, to confirm healing and exclude cancer.
Testing too soon after antibiotics and while on a PPI suppresses urease activity and risks a false-negative result.

questions.stem: John's gastroscopy shows mild antral gastritis with H. pylori on biopsy and an 8 mm ulcer in the duodenal bulb. Which mechanism best explains how antral-predominant H. pylori infection promotes duodenal ulceration?
options: Loss of antral D-cell somatostatin, raising gastrin and gastric acid output
Destruction of corpus parietal cells, causing hypochlorhydria and mucosal atrophy
Inhibition of mucosal COX-1, reducing prostaglandin-driven mucus and bicarbonate
Increased vagal tone from stress, directly driving parietal cell acid secretion
questions.why: Antral H. pylori inflammation reduces somatostatin from D cells, which removes the brake on G-cell gastrin. More gastrin drives more acid, and the extra acid reaching the duodenum causes gastric metaplasia there and ulceration.
notes: Corpus-predominant gastritis with parietal cell loss lowers acid output; it is linked to gastric ulcer, atrophy and cancer, not to duodenal ulcer.
This is how NSAIDs damage the mucosa. It is contributing in John, but it does not explain how H. pylori causes an ulcer.
Stress may make symptoms worse, but it is not the mechanism by which antral H. pylori infection raises acid and causes duodenal ulcer.

questions.stem: John's 8 mm duodenal bulb ulcer is on the anterior wall, where the main risk is perforation into the peritoneal cavity. If it had been on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum, which artery could it erode into and cause major haemorrhage?
questions.why: The gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, runs directly behind the first part of the duodenum. Posterior duodenal bulb ulcers therefore cause brisk bleeding, while anterior ulcers tend to perforate.
notes: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature, so it is at risk from lesser-curve gastric ulcers, not duodenal ulcers.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas behind the stomach, so it is at risk from posterior gastric ulcers that penetrate into the lesser sac.
The superior mesenteric artery crosses in front of the third part of the duodenum, well away from the duodenal bulb.
